On the day the Wang Jingwei government printed 'The Chongqing Blue Shirts' Shanghai District Organization and Its Roster' in the Zhonghua Ribao, Gu Shenyan gave the order to burn the whole of the Huaxing Trading Company. He had not foreseen the disaster. The fire ran down from the top floor of the Xianghu Building and soon had the entire tower. Amid the wail of the fire engines he stood a long time at a street-facing window of the New World Hotel, the flames on the far building leaping and leaping in his eyes.
Gu Shenyan turned his head slowly to the subordinates standing behind him, heads bowed. "You must remember this day."

It was the 28th of November, 1941. The Juntong's ten sections, eight action squads, and five intelligence groups across the Shanghai region were all blown. Ordered back to Chongqing, Gu Shenyan chose to stay. "To give up Shanghai," he told Lin Nansheng, "is to put out one of our own eyes."
"To stay in Shanghai is to disobey Mr. Dai's order," Lin Nansheng reminded him, carefully.

"Have you ever asked yourself how we came to this?" Gu Shenyan looked at him and let out a long breath. "Once an organization makes loyalty to a man, or to a clique, its whole reason for being, a day like today can't be helped." Lin Nansheng did not know what to say. Gu Shenyan put on the felt hat he had been turning in his hand. He would go to Hangzhou, and to Nanjing, to recruit fresh hands. "Your task," he said at the last, "is to wait for me to come back."

That night Lin Nansheng burst into the garret where Zhu Yizhen lived, in the uniform of the Peace Army, one arm bandaged and slung from his neck, like a young officer slipped out of an army hospital in search of a night's pleasure.
"You haven't thrown all my clothes out, I hope?" Lin Nansheng said it to Zhu Yizhen, smiling. "I mean to stay a few days."
Zhu Yizhen could not smile. All evening she had sat at the frame reading that copy of the Zhonghua Ribao, and now her eyes came to rest on Lin Nansheng's slung arm.

"It's nothing." Still smiling, Lin Nansheng tore the bandage off and looked round at the four walls. "More like a home now than it was at first." Zhu Yizhen would not speak. She took a set of pajamas from the cupboard, laid them on the bed, then sat at the frame, breathed on her cold-stiff hands, and took up the needle.

It was a strange night. Now and then the far wail of a siren came through the window, but inside there was only the sound of thread through silk. Lin Nansheng lay on the bed a while, then threw off the quilt and stood barefoot on the floor. Zhu Yizhen spoke at last, her eyes on the half-worked butterfly. "You should be getting out, not coming here."
"Someone always has to stay." Lin Nansheng hesitated, then went and laid both hands on her shoulders, kneading them like a masseur. "You can't sit up till dawn."
Zhu Yizhen freed herself gently. "One night is nothing. Tomorrow I'll buy bedding."
Lin Nansheng went back to the bed without a sound. "I shouldn't have come."
Zhu Yizhen gave a small smile. "Sleep well."

A few days later the Japanese army took the whole concession. From first light the planes wheeled low and leaflets came down in clouds like snow; yet the streets of the Japanese quarter were strangely clean and deserted, only the puttee-wrapped Chinese police pacing in the cold wind. Toward noon Zhu Yizhen went out, and soon came back.
"Japan has declared war on Britain and America." She was a little breathless in the doorway. "This morning they sank the gunboat Peterel where it lay moored in the Huangpu."
With that she took off her Western dress, changed into a cheongsam, and quickly put her hair up at the mirror.
Leaning at the window, Lin Nansheng watched her. "Can you get out of Shanghai today?"
Zhu Yizhen was taken aback. "Out or not, I have to." She turned, wrung a towel, wiped the paint from her face. "There's half a loaf in the drawer."
As she opened the door Lin Nansheng stopped her. "Let me go in your place."
Zhu Yizhen smiled. "That's impossible."
"Then let me come with you."
"That too is impossible."
"And if I had a way out of the city?"

Zhu Yizhen said no more, only raised her eyes and looked hard at him. But the two of them did not walk like people in a hurry to leave the city; they walked like a young officer strolling with his sweetheart. At a telephone box Lin Nansheng went in and made a call, then came out, his arm again at her waist, and took her to a sake house by the road.
Now and then a troop truck packed with Japanese soldiers rolled down the avenue; they were crossing Suzhou Creek into the heart of Shanghai.
Zhu Yizhen looked at the cups and plates. "How long would you have me wait?"
Lin Nansheng said nothing. He drank sip by sip and ate bite by bite, until a black Nissan drew up at the door. Then he set down his chopsticks and stood. "Let's go."

Zhu Yizhen knew this car, and the toothbrush-mustached Japanese at the wheel. This time, though, once they were in, he did not start the engine. "We're finished," he said to Lin Nansheng, in fluent Chinese. "You said we wouldn't meet again."
"Can't you do a friend one favor?" Lin Nansheng said, smiling.
"We're not friends." He watched a military truck pass beyond the glass. "I could kill the two of you right now."

"Better call it one more piece of business." Still smiling, Lin Nansheng drew out a small key and slid it from behind into the man's pocket. "There's a safe-deposit box at the Central Reserve Bank. See us out of the city and what's in it is yours."
The toothbrush mustache did not move; the right hand in his inside pocket never let go of the pistol.
Lin Nansheng patted his shoulder, still smiling. "Kobayashi. Killing a man takes courage."
Kobayashi Daisuke stared at Lin Nansheng's face in the rearview mirror a good while. "Lin-san, in that uniform, once they catch you, you'll be shot."
The smile froze on Lin Nansheng's face. He shut his eyes and leaned back. "Drive," he said, quietly.

Kobayashi Daisuke was a second secretary at the Japanese consulate in Shanghai. From the first time he traded intelligence with Lin Nansheng, he had known he had already lost his country, the way he had lost his wife and child. They had died in a car accident, the driver a drunken marine lieutenant. A few weeks later, on the very night the lieutenant walked free from the courtroom, he set a pistol under his own jaw. In the end he did not pull the trigger.

Well past the last checkpoint, the black Nissan pulled up at the edge of a lonely lane. Lin Nansheng said nothing; when he had seen Zhu Yizhen out, he drew his pistol and pressed it to the back of Kobayashi Daisuke's neck.
"You know I'm not afraid to die." Both hands on the wheel, Kobayashi Daisuke said it calmly. "Life stopped meaning anything to me long ago."
Lin Nansheng sighed. "Get out."

Obediently Kobayashi Daisuke got out, went to the trunk, and opened it himself. Then he turned to the black muzzle, his eyes on Lin Nansheng, and drew out one by one everything on him that could name him, dropping it all at his feet, the little key with it. He raised his head, looked a last time at the leaden sky, and climbed into the trunk, closing his eyes as if to sleep. In the instant the shot came, he saw his wife and his young son.

When Zhu Yizhen ran back to the car, Lin Nansheng was crouched on the ground, gathering up one by one Kobayashi Daisuke's wallet, papers, pistol, watch, ring, and that little key, and dropping them into his pocket.
"What did you come back for?" Lin Nansheng looked up at her. "If it were I who had died, you'd never have got away."
"If he meant to kill us, he needn't have waited till we were out of the city."
"He'd have done it sooner or later." Lin Nansheng stood and put the little key in Zhu Yizhen's hand. "Keep it safe. It's the key to your drawer."

Zhu Yizhen understood at once: there had never been a safe-deposit box at the bank. He was only an agent at the end of his rope now. After a moment she opened the passenger door and got in, and looked at Lin Nansheng's ever-paler face. "You didn't have to help me like this."
"It isn't to help you." Lin Nansheng turned his head to the bare fields. "I do it for myself."

At nightfall they parted before a ruined temple at a fork of two roads. Zhu Yizhen went to find her organization and pass on what she carried; Lin Nansheng drove to the dyke along the Taipu River, where a thin, scattered snow began to fall out of the night sky. He opened the trunk, went over the body, then took Kobayashi Daisuke's wallet, papers, pistol, watch, and ring from his own pocket and threw them one by one into the river. Last of all he slipped the car out of gear and heaved it in after them.

Tired and hungry, Lin Nansheng got back to the temple deep in the night, but Zhu Yizhen was not waiting inside. Only toward noon the next day did she come up the path from far off, a bundle over her arm, her overcoat and cheongsam changed now for a short padded jacket.
Zhu Yizhen handed Lin Nansheng the bundle: two pieces of rice cake and a man's padded jacket. "Eat, and change," she said. "Those clothes draw too much notice."

That night, on the way back to Shanghai, they put up at an inn, and like a couple long married they washed in silence and lay down in silence. In six years it was the first time they had lain side by side under one quilt, both of them careful, careful even later, when they made love. They held their breath as well as they could. Afterward Lin Nansheng said in her ear, "Tell me. How have you lived these six years?"
Zhu Yizhen did not speak. In the dark she clenched her teeth hard, until Lin Nansheng pried them apart with his tongue, and then she let one long breath go into his mouth.
At first light Zhu Yizhen said, suddenly, "I have a husband."
Lin Nansheng's eyes went wide, but he soon found the answer in hers. "But he's already dead."
